name: career-technical-openquiz-next-foundations
description: 按 Career OS JD 缺口补充的公开技术测评原题；题干、选项和解释均直接来自 Open Quiz Commons，不新增原创题。覆盖 Python 异步与标准库、JavaScript/Node.js 网络、Rust 并发/FFI/工具链、边缘限流与部署。

source.selection_basis: Career OS jobs 表的 software-testing-ops、technical-support-fae、iot-embedded、data-analysis、ai-rag 题型缺口映射

questions.category: Python 工程基础（迭代器与生成器）
questions.title: What is an iterator in Python?
options: A. A function that returns multiple values
B. An object that represents a stream of data
D. A data type for collections
questions.explanation: An iterator is an object that represents a stream of data and implements the __iter__() and __next__() methods.
questions.source_text: What is an iterator in Python?

questions.category: Python 工程基础（迭代器与生成器）
questions.title: Which method is used to get the next item from an iterator?
questions.explanation: The built-in next() function calls the iterator’s __next__() method to retrieve the next item.
questions.source_text: Which method is used to get the next item from an iterator?

questions.category: Python 工程基础（迭代器与生成器）
questions.title: What happens when an iterator is exhausted?
questions.explanation: When an iterator has no more items to return, it raises a StopIteration exception.
questions.source_text: What happens when an iterator is exhausted?

questions.category: Python 工程基础（迭代器与生成器）
questions.title: Which keyword is used to create a generator in Python?
questions.explanation: The yield keyword turns a function into a generator, producing values one at a time while preserving state.
questions.source_text: Which keyword is used to create a generator in Python?

questions.category: Python 工程基础（迭代器与生成器）
questions.title: What does calling a generator function return?
questions.explanation: Calling a generator function returns a generator object, which is a type of iterator.
questions.source_text: What does calling a generator function return?

questions.category: Python 工程基础（迭代器与生成器）
questions.title: Which of the following is a generator expression?
options: D. x * 2 for x in range(5)
questions.explanation: A generator expression uses parentheses and creates a generator that yields values lazily.
questions.source_text: Which of the following is a generator expression?

questions.category: Python 工程基础（迭代器与生成器）
questions.title: Why are generators considered memory-efficient?
options: A. They store all values in memory
B. They execute faster than loops
C. They produce values on demand
D. They use compiled code internally
questions.explanation: Generators yield values one at a time and do not store the entire sequence in memory.
questions.source_text: Why are generators considered memory-efficient?

questions.category: Python 工程基础（迭代器与生成器）
questions.title: Which built-in function can be used to manually iterate over an iterator?
questions.explanation: The next() function retrieves the next value from an iterator until StopIteration is raised.
questions.source_text: Which built-in function can be used to manually iterate over an iterator?

questions.category: Python 工程基础（迭代器与生成器）
questions.title: Which statement about iterators is TRUE?
options: A. Iterators can be reused indefinitely
C. Iterators maintain state between iterations
questions.explanation: Iterators maintain internal state and remember where they are during iteration.
questions.source_text: Which statement about iterators is TRUE?

questions.category: Python 工程基础（迭代器与生成器）
questions.title: Which of the following can be iterated over using a for loop?
questions.explanation: Any iterable object (such as lists, tuples, strings, and generators) can be used in a for loop.
questions.source_text: Which of the following can be iterated over using a for loop?

questions.title: Which module in the Python standard library is used to work with dates and times?
questions.explanation: The datetime module provides classes for working with dates, times, and date-time combinations. dateutil is a third-party library, not part of the standard library.
questions.source_text: Which module in the Python standard library is used to work with dates and times?

questions.title: Which standard library module allows you to generate random numbers?
questions.explanation: The random module provides functions for generating pseudo-random numbers and making random selections.
questions.source_text: Which standard library module allows you to generate random numbers?

questions.title: Which module is commonly used to interact with the operating system, such as reading environment variables or working with file paths?
questions.explanation: The os module provides a portable way to interact with the operating system, including environment variables, directory handling, and process management.
questions.source_text: Which module is commonly used to interact with the operating system, such as reading environment variables or working with file paths?

questions.title: Which module provides access to command-line arguments passed to a Python script?
questions.explanation: The sys module exposes sys.argv, which contains the list of command-line arguments passed to the script.
questions.source_text: Which module provides access to command-line arguments passed to a Python script?

questions.title: Which standard library module is best suited for parsing command-line arguments in a user-friendly way?
questions.explanation: argparse is the recommended standard library module for parsing command-line arguments and generating help messages.
questions.source_text: Which standard library module is best suited for parsing command-line arguments in a user-friendly way?

questions.title: Which module is used for working with regular expressions in Python?
questions.explanation: The re module provides support for regular expressions. regex is a third-party alternative.
questions.source_text: Which module is used for working with regular expressions in Python?

questions.title: Which standard library module allows serialization and deserialization of Python objects?
questions.explanation: The pickle module is used to serialize and deserialize Python objects, allowing them to be saved to or loaded from files.
questions.source_text: Which standard library module allows serialization and deserialization of Python objects?

questions.title: Which module should be used to safely handle passwords, tokens, or cryptographic secrets?
questions.explanation: The secrets module is designed for generating cryptographically strong random numbers suitable for managing passwords and security tokens.
questions.source_text: Which module should be used to safely handle passwords, tokens, or cryptographic secrets?

questions.title: Which standard library module provides mathematical functions such as sin(), cos(), and sqrt()?
questions.explanation: The math module provides access to mathematical functions for real numbers, including trigonometry and square roots.
questions.source_text: Which standard library module provides mathematical functions such as sin(), cos(), and sqrt()?

questions.title: Which module helps measure the execution time of small bits of Python code?
questions.explanation: The timeit module is specifically designed to measure the execution time of small code snippets accurately.
questions.source_text: Which module helps measure the execution time of small bits of Python code?

questions.title: Which standard library module provides tools for working with JSON data?
questions.explanation: The json module allows encoding Python objects to JSON format and decoding JSON back into Python objects.
questions.source_text: Which standard library module provides tools for working with JSON data?

questions.title: Which module provides utilities for copying files and directory trees?
questions.explanation: The shutil module offers high-level file operations such as copying, moving, and deleting files and directories.
questions.source_text: Which module provides utilities for copying files and directory trees?

questions.title: Which keyword is used to define a coroutine function in Python for asynchronous programming?
questions.explanation: The `async def` syntax defines a function as a coroutine, which can then be scheduled and run by an event loop.
questions.source_text: Which keyword is used to define a coroutine function in Python for asynchronous programming?

questions.title: What is the primary role of the Event Loop in `asyncio`?
options: A. To speed up CPU-bound calculations
B. To manage and schedule the execution of various tasks and IO operations
C. To automatically compile Python code to machine language
D. To provide a multi-threaded lock for shared memory
questions.explanation: The Event Loop is the core of every asyncio application; it schedules coroutines, handles network IO, and manages subprocesses.
questions.source_text: What is the primary role of the Event Loop in `asyncio`?

questions.title: Which keyword is used to pause the execution of a coroutine until a result is returned from another coroutine or future?
questions.explanation: `await` passes control back to the event loop, suspending the current coroutine until the awaited object yields a result.
questions.source_text: Which keyword is used to pause the execution of a coroutine until a result is returned from another coroutine or future?

questions.title: How do you run the main entry point coroutine in a modern `asyncio` script (Python 3.7+)?
questions.explanation: `asyncio.run()` is the high-level entry point that handles creating the event loop, running the coroutine, and closing the loop.
questions.source_text: How do you run the main entry point coroutine in a modern `asyncio` script (Python 3.7+)?

questions.title: What is the benefit of using `asyncio.gather()`?
options: A. It runs coroutines sequentially in a specific order
B. It runs multiple concurrent tasks and waits for them to finish
C. It converts synchronous functions into asynchronous ones
D. It prevents race conditions in multi-threaded code
questions.explanation: `asyncio.gather()` allows multiple awaitables to be scheduled concurrently, returning their results as a list once all are complete.
questions.source_text: What is the benefit of using `asyncio.gather()`?

questions.title: In asynchronous networking, what does a 'Future' object represent?
options: A. A result that has already been calculated
B. An eventual result of an asynchronous operation
C. A callback function for error handling
D. A historical log of previous IO calls
questions.explanation: A `Future` is a low-level object that acts as a placeholder for a result that will be available in the future.
questions.source_text: In asynchronous networking, what does a 'Future' object represent?

questions.title: Which function is used to create a network server that handles connections asynchronously?
questions.explanation: `asyncio.start_server()` creates and starts a TCP stream server, calling a specific callback for every new client connection.
questions.source_text: Which function is used to create a network server that handles connections asynchronously?

questions.title: When writing an async client, what do `asyncio.open_connection()` return?
options: B. A tuple of (reader, writer) streams
D. A list of available ports
questions.explanation: It returns a pair of `(StreamReader, StreamWriter)` objects, which provide high-level async methods for reading and writing data.
questions.source_text: When writing an async client, what do `asyncio.open_connection()` return?

questions.title: What is a 'Task' in the context of `asyncio`?
options: A. A background process running in a separate CPU core
B. An object that wraps a coroutine and schedules its execution
questions.explanation: Tasks are used to schedule coroutines concurrently. When a coroutine is wrapped into a Task with `asyncio.create_task()`, it is automatically scheduled to run soon.
questions.source_text: What is a 'Task' in the context of `asyncio`?

questions.title: What happens if you perform a blocking synchronous operation (like `time.sleep()`) inside an async function?
options: A. Asyncio automatically converts it to async
B. It blocks the entire event loop, stopping all other tasks
D. It runs in a separate thread automatically
questions.explanation: Blocking the event loop with synchronous calls prevents other coroutines from running. For delays, `await asyncio.sleep()` should be used instead.
questions.source_text: What happens if you perform a blocking synchronous operation (like `time.sleep()`) inside an async function?

questions.title: Which method is used to wrap a blocking synchronous function so it can be run in a separate thread without blocking the event loop?
questions.explanation: `run_in_executor()` allows you to run CPU-bound or blocking IO code in a thread pool (or process pool) so the event loop remains free.
questions.source_text: Which method is used to wrap a blocking synchronous function so it can be run in a separate thread without blocking the event loop?

questions.title: What is the purpose of `async with` syntax?
options: A. To loop through an asynchronous iterator
B. To manage resources (like network connections) using an asynchronous context manager
C. To speed up file system access
D. To define an anonymous coroutine
questions.explanation: `async with` is used for asynchronous context managers that need to perform IO when entering or exiting the context (e.g., closing a database connection).
questions.source_text: What is the purpose of `async with` syntax?

questions.title: What does asynchronous code allow JavaScript to do?
options: A. Run multiple threads in parallel
B. Execute long-running tasks without blocking the main thread
questions.explanation: Asynchronous code allows long-running operations to run without blocking the main execution thread.
questions.source_text: What does asynchronous code allow JavaScript to do?

questions.title: Which pattern was commonly used for async operations before Promises?
questions.explanation: Callbacks were the primary way to handle asynchronous operations before Promises were introduced.
questions.source_text: Which pattern was commonly used for async operations before Promises?

questions.title: What problem is commonly associated with deeply nested callbacks?
questions.explanation: Deeply nested callbacks reduce readability and maintainability, a problem known as callback hell.
questions.source_text: What problem is commonly associated with deeply nested callbacks?

questions.title: What does a Promise represent?
options: B. A value that may be available in the future
C. A thread running in parallel
questions.explanation: A Promise represents a value that will be fulfilled or rejected at some point in the future.
questions.source_text: What does a Promise represent?

questions.title: Which method is used to handle a fulfilled Promise?
questions.explanation: `then()` is used to handle the resolved value of a Promise.
questions.source_text: Which method is used to handle a fulfilled Promise?

questions.title: Which method is used to handle errors in a Promise chain?
questions.explanation: `catch()` handles rejected Promises or errors thrown in the chain.
questions.source_text: Which method is used to handle errors in a Promise chain?

questions.title: What keyword is used to pause execution until a Promise resolves?
questions.explanation: `await` pauses execution of an async function until the Promise settles.
questions.source_text: What keyword is used to pause execution until a Promise resolves?

questions.title: Where can the `await` keyword be used?
questions.explanation: `await` can only be used inside functions declared with the `async` keyword.
questions.source_text: Where can the `await` keyword be used?

questions.title: What does an async function always return?
questions.explanation: An async function always returns a Promise, even if it returns a plain value.
questions.source_text: What does an async function always return?

questions.title: Which construct is commonly used to handle errors with async/await?
questions.explanation: `try...catch` is used to handle errors in async/await code.
questions.source_text: Which construct is commonly used to handle errors with async/await?

questions.title: Which statement is used to handle runtime errors in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: JavaScript handles runtime errors using the try...catch statement.
questions.source_text: Which statement is used to handle runtime errors in JavaScript?

questions.title: What type of error occurs when JavaScript code has invalid syntax?
questions.explanation: SyntaxError occurs when the JavaScript engine encounters invalid syntax.
questions.source_text: What type of error occurs when JavaScript code has invalid syntax?

questions.title: Which error is thrown when accessing a variable that has not been declared?
questions.explanation: ReferenceError occurs when a variable is not defined in the current scope.
questions.source_text: Which error is thrown when accessing a variable that has not been declared?

questions.title: What does the finally block do in try...catch...finally?
options: A. Runs only if an error occurs
B. Runs only if no error occurs
C. Always runs regardless of error
questions.explanation: The finally block always executes, whether an error occurs or not.
questions.source_text: What does the finally block do in try...catch...finally?

questions.title: Which keyword is used to manually raise an error in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: The throw keyword is used to create custom errors in JavaScript.
questions.source_text: Which keyword is used to manually raise an error in JavaScript?

questions.title: What type of error occurs when calling a method on null or undefined?
questions.explanation: TypeError occurs when an operation is performed on an incompatible value like null or undefined.
questions.source_text: What type of error occurs when calling a method on null or undefined?

questions.title: Which built-in object is commonly used for debugging output?
questions.explanation: The console object is used for debugging via methods like console.log().
questions.source_text: Which built-in object is commonly used for debugging output?

questions.title: Which console method is best suited for printing error messages?
questions.explanation: console.error() is specifically intended for error messages.
questions.source_text: Which console method is best suited for printing error messages?

questions.title: What happens if an exception is thrown and not caught?
options: D. The error is logged automatically
questions.explanation: An uncaught exception stops JavaScript execution and may crash the script.
questions.source_text: What happens if an exception is thrown and not caught?

questions.title: Which statement is commonly used to inspect program flow during debugging?
questions.explanation: console.log() is widely used to inspect values and program flow during debugging.
questions.source_text: Which statement is commonly used to inspect program flow during debugging?

questions.title: Which Node.js module is primarily used to create HTTP servers?
questions.explanation: The 'http' module in Node.js provides the functionality to create HTTP servers and clients.
questions.source_text: Which Node.js module is primarily used to create HTTP servers?

questions.title: What is the default port number for HTTP servers?
questions.explanation: Port 80 is the default port for HTTP servers, while 443 is the default for HTTPS.
questions.source_text: What is the default port number for HTTP servers?

questions.title: Which method of the http.ServerResponse object is used to send data back to the client?
questions.explanation: The 'write()' method is used to send data chunks to the client before ending the response.
questions.source_text: Which method of the http.ServerResponse object is used to send data back to the client?

questions.title: What does the 'end()' method of http.ServerResponse do?
options: C. Closes the TCP connection immediately
D. Flushes the buffer without ending
questions.explanation: The 'end()' method signals that the response is complete and no more data will be sent.
questions.source_text: What does the 'end()' method of http.ServerResponse do?

questions.title: Which property of the IncomingMessage object contains the HTTP request headers?
questions.explanation: The 'headers' property of IncomingMessage stores all the HTTP request headers.
questions.source_text: Which property of the IncomingMessage object contains the HTTP request headers?

questions.title: How can you parse the URL of an incoming HTTP request in Node.js?
questions.explanation: The 'url' module provides the 'url.parse()' method to parse request URLs.
questions.source_text: How can you parse the URL of an incoming HTTP request in Node.js?

questions.title: Which status code represents 'Not Found' in HTTP?
questions.explanation: HTTP status code 404 indicates that the requested resource could not be found.
questions.source_text: Which status code represents 'Not Found' in HTTP?

questions.title: What is the purpose of the 'Content-Type' header in HTTP responses?
options: A. Specifies the size of the content
B. Specifies the type of the content being sent
C. Specifies the encoding of the connection
questions.explanation: The 'Content-Type' header tells the client the media type of the resource, such as text/html or application/json.
questions.source_text: What is the purpose of the 'Content-Type' header in HTTP responses?

questions.title: Which Node.js module is used to handle secure HTTPS connections?
questions.explanation: The 'https' module is a variant of the 'http' module that supports SSL/TLS for secure communication.
questions.source_text: Which Node.js module is used to handle secure HTTPS connections?

questions.title: What does the HTTP status code 500 represent?
questions.explanation: Status code 500 indicates an Internal Server Error, meaning something went wrong on the server side.
questions.source_text: What does the HTTP status code 500 represent?

questions.title: Which global object provides access to environment variables in Node.js?
questions.explanation: Environment variables are accessed through the process.env object in Node.js.
questions.source_text: Which global object provides access to environment variables in Node.js?

questions.title: What is the purpose of NODE_ENV in Node.js applications?
options: A. To specify the Node.js version
B. To define the environment mode like development or production
questions.explanation: NODE_ENV is commonly used to distinguish between development and production environments.
questions.source_text: What is the purpose of NODE_ENV in Node.js applications?

questions.title: Which method returns the current working directory of a Node.js process?
questions.explanation: process.cwd() returns the current working directory of the Node.js process.
questions.source_text: Which method returns the current working directory of a Node.js process?

questions.title: How can you set an environment variable when starting a Node.js application?
options: B. By passing it in the command line before node
C. By editing the Node.js source code
questions.explanation: Environment variables can be set in the shell before running node, e.g., NODE_ENV=production node app.js.
questions.source_text: How can you set an environment variable when starting a Node.js application?

questions.title: Which property of process provides the absolute path of the Node.js executable?
questions.explanation: process.execPath gives the absolute path of the Node.js executable.
questions.source_text: Which property of process provides the absolute path of the Node.js executable?

questions.title: What does process.exit(0) indicate?
options: A. The process exited with an error
questions.explanation: An exit code of 0 indicates successful termination of the process.
questions.source_text: What does process.exit(0) indicate?

questions.title: Which module is often used to manage configuration files in Node.js?
questions.explanation: The 'config' module is commonly used to manage configuration files and environment-specific settings.
questions.source_text: Which module is often used to manage configuration files in Node.js?

questions.title: What does process.env return if an environment variable is not set?
questions.explanation: If an environment variable is not set, process.env returns undefined for that key.
questions.source_text: What does process.env return if an environment variable is not set?

questions.title: Which property of process provides the current Node.js version?
questions.explanation: process.version returns the current Node.js version as a string.
questions.source_text: Which property of process provides the current Node.js version?

questions.title: Which method can be used to change the current working directory of a Node.js process?
questions.explanation: process.chdir() changes the current working directory of the Node.js process.
questions.source_text: Which method can be used to change the current working directory of a Node.js process?

questions.title: What keyword is used to define an asynchronous function in Rust?
questions.explanation: In Rust, asynchronous functions are defined using the `async fn` keyword.
questions.source_text: What keyword is used to define an asynchronous function in Rust?

questions.title: Which trait must a type implement to be awaitable in Rust?
questions.explanation: The `Future` trait represents values that are computed asynchronously and can be awaited.
questions.source_text: Which trait must a type implement to be awaitable in Rust?

questions.title: What does the `.await` syntax do in Rust async programming?
options: A. Blocks the thread until the Future finishes
B. Polls the Future and yields control if not ready
questions.explanation: Using `.await` polls a Future, yields control to the executor if not ready, and resumes when complete.
questions.source_text: What does the `.await` syntax do in Rust async programming?

questions.title: Which of the following crates is commonly used as an async runtime in Rust?
questions.explanation: `tokio` is a widely used asynchronous runtime for Rust, providing async I/O, task scheduling, and more.
questions.source_text: Which of the following crates is commonly used as an async runtime in Rust?

questions.title: What is the purpose of the 'Send' trait in Rust's concurrency context?
options: A. Ensures a type can be safely sent to another thread
questions.explanation: The `Send` trait marks types that can be safely transferred ownership to another thread.
questions.source_text: What is the purpose of the 'Send' trait in Rust's concurrency context?

questions.title: Which Rust feature allows multiple tasks to run concurrently without using OS threads?
questions.explanation: Async/await enables lightweight tasks that the runtime multiplexes onto fewer OS threads.
questions.source_text: Which Rust feature allows multiple tasks to run concurrently without using OS threads?

questions.title: In Rust's async model, what drives a future to completion?
questions.explanation: An executor or runtime schedules and polls futures to make progress until they complete.
questions.source_text: In Rust's async model, what drives a future to completion?

questions.title: Which mechanism does Rust use for safe shared mutable state in async code?
questions.explanation: `Mutex<T>` provides safe shared mutable access by allowing only one mutable borrow at a time with locking.
questions.source_text: Which mechanism does Rust use for safe shared mutable state in async code?

questions.title: What enables multiple tasks to communicate asynchronously in Rust?
questions.explanation: Channels are used to send values between tasks safely and asynchronously.
questions.source_text: What enables multiple tasks to communicate asynchronously in Rust?

questions.title: How do you spawn an asynchronous task on the Tokio runtime?
questions.explanation: `tokio::spawn` is used to spawn asynchronous tasks onto the Tokio runtime.
questions.source_text: How do you spawn an asynchronous task on the Tokio runtime?

questions.title: In Rust, which trait is used to define behavior for types that can be compared for equality?
questions.explanation: PartialEq is the trait used to allow equality comparisons using == and != operators.
questions.source_text: In Rust, which trait is used to define behavior for types that can be compared for equality?

questions.title: What is the primary purpose of generics in Rust?
options: B. To enable code reuse for multiple types
C. To allocate data on the heap
questions.explanation: Generics enable writing code that works with any data type while maintaining type safety.
questions.source_text: What is the primary purpose of generics in Rust?

questions.title: Which syntax correctly defines a generic function in Rust?
questions.explanation: The correct syntax uses angle brackets: fn foo<T>(x: T) {}.
questions.source_text: Which syntax correctly defines a generic function in Rust?

questions.title: How do you constrain a generic type to only those implementing the Debug trait?
options: C. fn foo<T where T: Debug>(x: T) {}
questions.explanation: Both fn foo<T: Debug>(x: T) {} and fn foo<T> where T: Debug (x: T) {} are valid to bound a generic by Debug.
questions.source_text: How do you constrain a generic type to only those implementing the Debug trait?

questions.title: Which trait should a type implement to support ordering comparisons in Rust?
questions.explanation: Ord requires total ordering, allowing the use of comparison methods like cmp().
questions.source_text: Which trait should a type implement to support ordering comparisons in Rust?

questions.title: What will happen if a generic function's type parameter does not satisfy the trait bounds required?
options: D. Program silently ignores the constraint
questions.explanation: Trait bounds are checked at compile time, so unsatisfied bounds cause compilation to fail.
questions.source_text: What will happen if a generic function's type parameter does not satisfy the trait bounds required?

questions.title: Which of the following is true about the Rust trait 'Copy'?
options: A. It allows types to be implicitly copied instead of moved
C. It is a marker trait for thread safety
D. It restricts types to be heap allocated
questions.explanation: 'Copy' trait allows types to be duplicated simply by copying bits, avoiding moves.
questions.source_text: Which of the following is true about the Rust trait 'Copy'?

questions.title: How do you specify multiple trait bounds on a generic type in a function signature?
options: A. fn foo<T: Debug + Clone>(x: T) {}
B. fn foo<T: Debug, Clone>(x: T) {}
C. fn foo<T>(x: T) where T: Debug + Clone {}
questions.explanation: You can specify with + syntax in angle brackets or via a where clause.
questions.source_text: How do you specify multiple trait bounds on a generic type in a function signature?

questions.title: What does it mean if a Rust trait has associated types?
options: A. The trait defines placeholder type names to be specified by implementors
B. The trait can only be used with structs
C. The trait automatically implements all generic types
questions.explanation: Associated types allow traits to define types that the implementor must specify.
questions.source_text: What does it mean if a Rust trait has associated types?

questions.title: What Rust feature allows you to write one struct to be generic over multiple types?
questions.explanation: Generics allow struct definitions to be parameterized with type variables.
questions.source_text: What Rust feature allows you to write one struct to be generic over multiple types?

questions.title: What keyword is used to declare a foreign function interface in Rust?
questions.explanation: The `extern` keyword declares foreign functions. `extern "C"` specifies the C calling convention.
questions.source_text: What keyword is used to declare a foreign function interface in Rust?

questions.title: Which block is required to call unsafe foreign functions in Rust?
questions.explanation: Calling foreign functions is inherently unsafe because Rust cannot verify their behavior. The `unsafe` block acknowledges this responsibility.
questions.source_text: Which block is required to call unsafe foreign functions in Rust?

questions.title: What is the correct way to represent a C `char*` string in Rust FFI?
questions.explanation: C strings are raw pointers (`*const c_char`). Use `CString::new()` for owned strings and `CStr::from_ptr()` for borrowed ones.
questions.source_text: What is the correct way to represent a C `char*` string in Rust FFI?

questions.title: Which attribute ensures a Rust struct has the same memory layout as a C struct?
questions.explanation: `#[repr(C)]` guarantees C-compatible field ordering, padding, and alignment. Essential for FFI struct compatibility.
questions.source_text: Which attribute ensures a Rust struct has the same memory layout as a C struct?

questions.title: How do you convert a Rust `String` to a C-compatible owned string?
questions.explanation: `CString::new()` creates a NUL-terminated owned string safe for FFI. It returns a `Result` to handle embedded NUL bytes.
questions.source_text: How do you convert a Rust `String` to a C-compatible owned string?

questions.title: What happens if a panic unwinds across an FFI boundary into C code?
options: B. The C code catches it as an exception
C. Rust automatically converts it to errno
D. The program prints a backtrace and exits cleanly
questions.explanation: Unwinding across FFI is undefined behavior. Use `std::panic::catch_unwind` or compile with `panic = "abort"` to prevent it.
questions.source_text: What happens if a panic unwinds across an FFI boundary into C code?

questions.title: Which type represents a raw mutable pointer in Rust?
questions.explanation: `*mut T` is a raw mutable pointer. Unlike references, raw pointers can be null, unaligned, and require `unsafe` to dereference.
questions.source_text: Which type represents a raw mutable pointer in Rust?

questions.title: What is the purpose of `bindgen` in Rust FFI projects?
options: A. Compile C code to WebAssembly
B. Generate Rust FFI bindings from C headers
C. Link Rust libraries into C programs
D. Validate memory safety of unsafe blocks
questions.explanation: `bindgen` parses C/C++ headers and generates Rust `extern` declarations, structs, and constants automatically.
questions.source_text: What is the purpose of `bindgen` in Rust FFI projects?

questions.title: When passing a callback function pointer to C, which trait bound is required for the Rust closure?
questions.explanation: Callback function pointers must have the `extern "C"` calling convention. Use `extern "C" fn(...)` function pointers, not closures directly.
questions.source_text: When passing a callback function pointer to C, which trait bound is required for the Rust closure?

questions.title: How should Rust code free memory allocated by a C library?
options: A. Call `drop()` on the raw pointer
B. Use `Box::from_raw()` and let it drop
C. Call the C library's corresponding free function
D. Rust's allocator automatically handles it
questions.explanation: Memory must be freed by the same allocator that allocated it. Always use the C library's provided free/dealloc function.
questions.source_text: How should Rust code free memory allocated by a C library?

questions.title: What does `#[no_mangle]` do on a Rust function?
options: A. Prevents the compiler from optimizing the function
B. Exports the function with its exact name for linking
C. Marks the function as unsafe
questions.explanation: `#[no_mangle]` preserves the function name in the symbol table, allowing C code to link to it by name.
questions.source_text: What does `#[no_mangle]` do on a Rust function?

questions.title: Which type should be used for a nullable function pointer in FFI signatures?
questions.explanation: `Option<extern "C" fn()>` represents a nullable function pointer (null = None). Rust optimizes this to a single pointer.
questions.source_text: Which type should be used for a nullable function pointer in FFI signatures?

questions.title: What is the correct way to handle C's `errno` in Rust?
options: A. Use `std::io::Error::last_os_error()` after a failing FFI call
B. Access the global `errno` variable directly
C. Check if the return value is -1 and panic
D. Rust automatically converts errno to Result
questions.explanation: Call `std::io::Error::last_os_error()` immediately after a failing FFI call to capture the platform's errno/GetLastError value.
questions.source_text: What is the correct way to handle C's `errno` in Rust?

questions.title: Which attribute makes a Rust type transparent (same ABI as its single field) for FFI?
questions.explanation: `#[repr(transparent)]` delegates ABI to the single non-ZST field, crucial for newtype wrappers around C types.
questions.source_text: Which attribute makes a Rust type transparent (same ABI as its single field) for FFI?

questions.title: What is the risk of implementing `Send`/`Sync` for a type wrapping a raw pointer from C?
options: A. It may violate thread safety if the C library isn't thread-safe
C. It prevents the type from being used in async code
D. It forces the type to be `'static`
questions.explanation: Implementing `Send`/`Sync` manually (via `unsafe impl`) asserts thread safety. If the underlying C library isn't thread-safe, this causes data races.
questions.source_text: What is the risk of implementing `Send`/`Sync` for a type wrapping a raw pointer from C?

questions.title: How do you correctly create a `CStr` reference from a raw pointer returned by C?
questions.explanation: `CStr::from_ptr` is unsafe because it trusts the pointer is valid, NUL-terminated, and lives long enough. Must be in an `unsafe` block.
questions.source_text: How do you correctly create a `CStr` reference from a raw pointer returned by C?

questions.title: What is the primary purpose of Clippy in the Rust ecosystem?
options: A. Code formatting and style enforcement
B. Static analysis and linting to catch common mistakes and improve code quality
D. Running unit and integration tests
questions.explanation: Clippy is a collection of lints to catch common mistakes and improve your Rust code. It performs static analysis, while rustfmt handles formatting.
questions.source_text: What is the primary purpose of Clippy in the Rust ecosystem?

questions.title: What is the primary purpose of rustfmt?
options: B. Code formatting according to community style guidelines
questions.explanation: rustfmt automatically formats Rust code according to the standard style guide. It ensures consistent formatting across a codebase.
questions.source_text: What is the primary purpose of rustfmt?

questions.title: How do you install Clippy and rustfmt using rustup?
options: A. rustup component add clippy rustfmt
D. They are installed by default with the stable toolchain
questions.explanation: Clippy and rustfmt are optional components installed via `rustup component add clippy rustfmt`. They are not installed by default with the minimal toolchain.
questions.source_text: How do you install Clippy and rustfmt using rustup?

questions.title: Which command runs Clippy lints on a Cargo project?
questions.explanation: `cargo clippy` runs Clippy lints on the current Cargo package. It accepts the same arguments as `cargo check`.
questions.source_text: Which command runs Clippy lints on a Cargo project?

questions.title: Which command formats a Cargo project using rustfmt?
questions.explanation: `cargo fmt` is the Cargo subcommand provided by rustfmt to format all crates in the workspace. `rustfmt` can also be run directly on files.
questions.source_text: Which command formats a Cargo project using rustfmt?

questions.title: How can you allow a specific Clippy lint (e.g., `needless_lifetimes`) for an entire crate?
options: A. Add `#![allow(clippy::needless_lifetimes)]` to the crate root
D. It is not possible to allow a lint crate-wide
questions.explanation: Crate-level lint attributes like `#![allow(clippy::needless_lifetimes)]` are placed in the crate root (usually `lib.rs` or `main.rs`).
questions.source_text: How can you allow a specific Clippy lint (e.g., `needless_lifetimes`) for an entire crate?

questions.title: What does the `rustfmt.toml` or `.rustfmt.toml` file control?
options: A. Which Clippy lints are enabled
B. Configuration options for rustfmt, such as max line width and indentation style
D. Editor integration settings for VS Code
questions.explanation: rustfmt reads configuration from `rustfmt.toml` (or `.rustfmt.toml`) to customize formatting rules like `max_width`, `indent_style`, `use_small_heuristics`, etc.
questions.source_text: What does the `rustfmt.toml` or `.rustfmt.toml` file control?

questions.title: Which Clippy lint group is enabled by default and includes lints for correctness, style, and complexity?
questions.explanation: The `clippy::correctness` group (often referred to as the default set) is enabled by default when running `cargo clippy`. It catches actual bugs or suspicious code. `clippy::style` and `clippy::complexity` are also enabled by default in practice, but the group name is not 'standard'.
questions.source_text: Which Clippy lint group is enabled by default and includes lints for correctness, style, and complexity?

questions.title: How do you run rustfmt in 'check' mode to verify formatting without modifying files (useful for CI)?
options: D. Both A and C are correct
questions.explanation: Both `cargo fmt --check` and `rustfmt --check` will exit with a non-zero status if formatting changes are needed, without writing them. This is standard for CI pipelines.
questions.source_text: How do you run rustfmt in 'check' mode to verify formatting without modifying files (useful for CI)?

questions.title: What is the effect of the Clippy lint `clippy::unwrap_used`?
options: A. It warns when `unwrap()` is called on `Option` or `Result`, suggesting explicit error handling
B. It suggests using `unwrap()` for cleaner code
D. It is part of the default lint set
questions.explanation: `clippy::unwrap_used` (from the `clippy::pedantic` group) warns against using `unwrap()` because it can panic. It encourages proper error handling with `?`, `match`, or `expect()` with a message.
questions.source_text: What is the effect of the Clippy lint `clippy::unwrap_used`?

questions.title: Which command updates rustfmt to the latest version available in the current toolchain?
questions.explanation: `rustup update` updates the entire toolchain, including the installed components like rustfmt and clippy. You don't update them individually via cargo.
questions.source_text: Which command updates rustfmt to the latest version available in the current toolchain?

questions.title: How can you temporarily disable a Clippy lint for a specific function or block?
options: A. Use `#[allow(clippy::lint_name)]` attribute on the item
D. It is not possible to disable locally
questions.explanation: Rust's lint attributes work on any item or statement. `#[allow(clippy::lint_name)]` placed directly above a function, block, or statement suppresses the lint for that scope.
questions.source_text: How can you temporarily disable a Clippy lint for a specific function or block?

questions.title: What does the `clippy::pedantic` lint group contain?
options: A. Only lints that are guaranteed to be correct and never produce false positives
B. Lints that are strict, opinionated, or may have false positives; off by default
C. Lints for performance optimization only
D. Lints that are deprecated and scheduled for removal
questions.explanation: The `pedantic` group contains lints that are very strict or opinionated (e.g., `unwrap_used`, `missing_docs_in_private_items`). They are not enabled by default because they may be noisy or have false positives. Enable with `#![warn(clippy::pedantic)]` or `cargo clippy -W clippy::pedantic`.
questions.source_text: What does the `clippy::pedantic` lint group contain?

questions.title: Which file does rustfmt ignore by default when formatting a project?
options: C. Files listed in `.rustfmtignore` (or `.gitignore` if no `.rustfmtignore` exists)
questions.explanation: rustfmt respects `.rustfmtignore` files with the same syntax as `.gitignore`. If `.rustfmtignore` doesn't exist, it falls back to `.gitignore`. It always skips the `target/` directory.
questions.source_text: Which file does rustfmt ignore by default when formatting a project?

questions.title: What is the recommended way to enforce formatting and linting in a CI pipeline?
options: A. Run `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy` and fail if they produce any output
B. Run `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`
C. Run `rustfmt --check` and `clippy -D warnings` directly on source files
D. Run `cargo test` which includes formatting and linting checks
questions.explanation: `cargo fmt --check` fails if formatting is needed. `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` treats all lints (including Clippy's) as errors, causing a non-zero exit code. This is the standard CI pattern.
questions.source_text: What is the recommended way to enforce formatting and linting in a CI pipeline?

questions.title: How do you configure Clippy lints per-project in `Cargo.toml`?
options: D. Clippy cannot be configured in Cargo.toml
questions.explanation: Since Cargo 1.80 (stabilized in 1.81), you can configure lints (including Clippy's) in `Cargo.toml` under `[workspace.lints]` or `[package.lints]` tables, e.g., `clippy::unwrap_used = "deny"`.
questions.source_text: How do you configure Clippy lints per-project in `Cargo.toml`?

questions.title: Which attribute marks a function as a unit test in Rust?
questions.explanation: The #[test] attribute tells Rust's test runner to treat the function as a test. It is part of the standard library's testing framework.
questions.source_text: Which attribute marks a function as a unit test in Rust?

questions.title: What macro is used to check that two values are equal in a test?
questions.explanation: assert_eq!(left, right) panics if the two values are not equal, printing both values. assert_ne! checks for inequality.
questions.source_text: What macro is used to check that two values are equal in a test?

questions.title: How do you indicate that a test should panic with a specific message?
questions.explanation: #[should_panic] marks a test as passing only if it panics. The optional `expected` parameter asserts the panic message contains that substring.
questions.source_text: How do you indicate that a test should panic with a specific message?

questions.title: Where are unit tests typically located in a Rust project?
options: A. In a separate `tests/` directory at the crate root
B. Inside the same file as the code they test, under a `mod tests { #[cfg(test)] ... }` module
questions.explanation: Unit tests live alongside the code in a `#[cfg(test)]` annotated module, usually named `tests`. Integration tests go in the `tests/` directory.
questions.source_text: Where are unit tests typically located in a Rust project?

questions.title: What does the `#[cfg(test)]` attribute do?
options: A. Runs the code only during `cargo bench`
B. Compiles the annotated item only when running tests (`cargo test`)
C. Marks the item as a benchmark function
D. Disables the item for release builds only
questions.explanation: `#[cfg(test)]` ensures the module or function is only compiled and included when `cargo test` runs, keeping test code out of production binaries.
questions.source_text: What does the `#[cfg(test)]` attribute do?

questions.title: Which command runs all tests in a Cargo project?
questions.explanation: `cargo test` compiles the crate in test mode and executes all functions annotated with #[test]. It also runs integration tests and doc tests.
questions.source_text: Which command runs all tests in a Cargo project?

questions.title: How can you run a specific test by name?
questions.explanation: `cargo test test_foo` filters tests whose names contain `test_foo`. You can also use `--` to pass arguments to the test binary, e.g., `cargo test -- --test-threads=1`.
questions.source_text: How can you run a specific test by name?

questions.title: What is the purpose of integration tests in Rust?
options: B. Test the public API of a crate as an external consumer would
C. Benchmark performance of internal functions
questions.explanation: Integration tests reside in `tests/` and only have access to the crate's public API, verifying the library works correctly from a user's perspective.
questions.source_text: What is the purpose of integration tests in Rust?

questions.title: Which crate is the de-facto standard for micro-benchmarking in Rust?
questions.explanation: The `criterion` crate provides statistically rigorous benchmarking, automatic outlier detection, and HTML reports. It works on stable Rust.
questions.source_text: Which crate is the de-facto standard for micro-benchmarking in Rust?

questions.title: How do you define a benchmark using the `criterion` crate?
options: B. fn bench_foo(c: &mut Criterion) { c.bench_function("foo", |b| b.iter(|| foo())); }
questions.explanation: Criterion uses a `criterion_group!` and `criterion_main!` macro setup. Benchmarks receive a `&mut Criterion` and use `bench_function` with a closure calling `iter`.
questions.source_text: How do you define a benchmark using the `criterion` crate?

questions.title: What does `cargo bench` do by default on stable Rust?
options: A. Runs all benchmarks defined with #[bench]
B. Compiles benchmarks but does not run them (benchmarks are unstable)
questions.explanation: The built-in `#[bench]` attribute and `Bencher` are unstable and require a nightly toolchain. On stable, `cargo bench` only compiles bench targets. Use `criterion` for stable benchmarking.
questions.source_text: What does `cargo bench` do by default on stable Rust?

questions.title: Which macro asserts that an expression returns a `Result::Err` variant?
questions.explanation: `assert_matches!(expr, Err(_))` from the standard library (since 1.68) or the `assert_matches` crate can pattern-match on `Result` variants. There is no dedicated `assert_err!` macro in std.
questions.source_text: Which macro asserts that an expression returns a `Result::Err` variant?

questions.title: What is the purpose of `#[ignore]` on a test function?
options: A. Marks the test as flaky
B. Excludes the test from default runs; run with `cargo test -- --ignored`
C. Runs the test only in release mode
D. Skips compilation of the test
questions.explanation: `#[ignore]` prevents the test from running during `cargo test`. Use `cargo test -- --ignored` to run only ignored tests, or `cargo test -- --include-ignored` to run all.
questions.source_text: What is the purpose of `#[ignore]` on a test function?

questions.title: How do you run tests with multiple threads disabled (single-threaded)?
questions.explanation: Pass `--test-threads=1` to the test binary via `cargo test -- --test-threads=1`. This is useful for tests that share global state or require deterministic ordering.
questions.source_text: How do you run tests with multiple threads disabled (single-threaded)?

questions.title: What does `cargo test --doc` do?
options: A. Generates documentation and runs examples in doc comments as tests
B. Tests only public API documentation
C. Runs benchmarks found in documentation
D. Validates markdown syntax in comments
questions.explanation: `cargo test --doc` (or just `cargo test` which includes doc tests by default) compiles and executes code blocks in documentation comments, ensuring examples stay correct.
questions.source_text: What does `cargo test --doc` do?

questions.title: Which testing approach generates random inputs to verify properties hold for a wide range of values?
questions.explanation: Property-based testing (e.g., with the `proptest` or `quickcheck` crates) automatically generates many random inputs to check that specified invariants always hold.
questions.source_text: Which testing approach generates random inputs to verify properties hold for a wide range of values?

questions.title: How can you share common setup/teardown logic across multiple tests?
options: A. Using a `setup()` function called manually in each test
B. Implementing `Drop` on a test fixture struct and creating it in each test
questions.explanation: Rust has no built-in test fixtures. The idiomatic pattern is a struct that implements `Drop` for teardown; instantiate it at the start of each test. The `Drop` impl runs when the test ends (even on panic).
questions.source_text: How can you share common setup/teardown logic across multiple tests?

questions.title: Which HTTP response status code is commonly used to indicate that a client has exceeded the allowed request rate?
questions.explanation: 429 Too Many Requests explicitly signals that the client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time.
questions.source_text: Which HTTP response status code is commonly used to indicate that a client has exceeded the allowed request rate?

questions.title: In AWS API Gateway, which feature enables you to throttle requests based on a quota or burst limit?
questions.explanation: Usage Plans let you define request quotas and burst limits per API key, providing built‑in rate limiting.
questions.source_text: In AWS API Gateway, which feature enables you to throttle requests based on a quota or burst limit?

questions.title: Which open‑source tool can be deployed as an edge proxy to enforce token bucket rate limiting for HTTP traffic?
questions.explanation: Envoy includes a token bucket filter that can be configured for per‑route rate limiting at the edge.
questions.source_text: Which open‑source tool can be deployed as an edge proxy to enforce token bucket rate limiting for HTTP traffic?

questions.title: A 'leaky bucket' algorithm differs from a 'token bucket' algorithm primarily in:
options: A. How it handles burst traffic
B. The data structure it uses
D. The type of HTTP methods it supports
questions.explanation: Leaky bucket smooths traffic to a constant rate, discarding excess bursts, while token bucket allows bursts up to a defined capacity.
questions.source_text: A 'leaky bucket' algorithm differs from a 'token bucket' algorithm primarily in:

questions.title: When implementing rate limiting in a serverless function (e.g., AWS Lambda), which service is best suited to store counters with low latency?
questions.explanation: DynamoDB provides fast, low‑latency reads/writes and supports atomic counters, making it ideal for distributed rate‑limit state.
questions.source_text: When implementing rate limiting in a serverless function (e.g., AWS Lambda), which service is best suited to store counters with low latency?

questions.title: Which Cloudflare feature can automatically return 429 responses for excessive requests to a domain?
questions.explanation: Cloudflare Rate Limiting Rules let you define thresholds and automatically block or challenge clients that exceed them.
questions.source_text: Which Cloudflare feature can automatically return 429 responses for excessive requests to a domain?

questions.title: In Kubernetes, which resource can be annotated to enable per‑pod rate limiting via istio‑pilot?
questions.explanation: Istio allows you to add annotations to Pods (or their containing Services) to apply Envoy‑level rate limits.
questions.source_text: In Kubernetes, which resource can be annotated to enable per‑pod rate limiting via istio‑pilot?

questions.title: What is the main advantage of using a distributed rate‑limiting algorithm like Consistent Hashing over a single node limiter?
options: C. Better scalability and fault tolerance
questions.explanation: Consistent hashing spreads counters across many nodes, avoiding a single point of failure and scaling horizontally.
questions.source_text: What is the main advantage of using a distributed rate‑limiting algorithm like Consistent Hashing over a single node limiter?

questions.title: Which of the following is NOT a typical dimension used when defining a rate‑limit key?
questions.explanation: Rate‑limit keys are usually derived from request attributes like IP, user ID, or method; hardware metrics like CPU temperature are irrelevant.
questions.source_text: Which of the following is NOT a typical dimension used when defining a rate‑limit key?

questions.title: When a rate‑limited request is retried after receiving a 429 response, which HTTP header often provides the wait time?
questions.explanation: The Retry-After header indicates how many seconds (or a date) the client should wait before retrying.
questions.source_text: When a rate‑limited request is retried after receiving a 429 response, which HTTP header often provides the wait time?

questions.title: Which Azure service offers built‑in rate limiting for HTTP APIs via policies?
questions.explanation: Azure API Management includes policies (e.g., check-header, rate-limit‑by‑key) that enforce request throttling.
questions.source_text: Which Azure service offers built‑in rate limiting for HTTP APIs via policies?

questions.title: In a serverless edge environment (e.g., Cloudflare Workers), which storage type is best for maintaining a short‑lived counter for rate limiting?
questions.explanation: Durable Objects provide low‑latency, strongly consistent state suitable for per‑client counters, while KV is eventually consistent.
questions.source_text: In a serverless edge environment (e.g., Cloudflare Workers), which storage type is best for maintaining a short‑lived counter for rate limiting?

questions.title: Which command is used to publish a Cloudflare Worker from the command line using Wrangler?
questions.explanation: The official CLI tool Wrangler uses the `wrangler deploy` command to upload and publish a Worker.
questions.source_text: Which command is used to publish a Cloudflare Worker from the command line using Wrangler?

questions.title: In a wrangler.toml file, which field defines the name of the script that will be executed for a Worker?
questions.explanation: The `main` field points to the JavaScript/TypeScript file that contains the Worker code.
questions.source_text: In a wrangler.toml file, which field defines the name of the script that will be executed for a Worker?

questions.title: What is the default route pattern applied when you bind a Worker to a zone without specifying a route?
options: D. No route – the Worker must be triggered manually
questions.explanation: If you publish a Worker without a custom route, it defaults to the catch‑all pattern `/*` for the specified zone.
questions.source_text: What is the default route pattern applied when you bind a Worker to a zone without specifying a route?

questions.title: Which Cloudflare feature allows a Worker to access KV storage with low latency at the edge?
questions.explanation: Workers KV (Key‑Value) is a globally replicated, low‑latency storage solution designed for Workers.
questions.source_text: Which Cloudflare feature allows a Worker to access KV storage with low latency at the edge?

questions.title: When using Wrangler, which command generates a new Worker project skeleton?
questions.explanation: `wrangler generate <name>` scaffolds a new Worker project with a starter template.
questions.source_text: When using Wrangler, which command generates a new Worker project skeleton?

questions.title: How can you restrict a Worker to only run on HTTP POST requests using the request method in the script?
questions.explanation: The HTTP method is available via `request.method`; compare it to the string "POST".
questions.source_text: How can you restrict a Worker to only run on HTTP POST requests using the request method in the script?

questions.title: Which of the following is NOT a supported language/runtime for Cloudflare Workers?
questions.explanation: Workers run on V8 and can execute WebAssembly modules (e.g., compiled from Rust). Python is not natively supported.
questions.source_text: Which of the following is NOT a supported language/runtime for Cloudflare Workers?

questions.title: What environment variable does Wrangler automatically set to indicate the name of the current zone during deployment?
questions.explanation: Wrangler injects `CF_ZONE_ID` (the numeric ID) and `CF_ZONE_NAME` (the domain) into the Worker environment.
questions.source_text: What environment variable does Wrangler automatically set to indicate the name of the current zone during deployment?

questions.title: Which Cloudflare product would you pair with Workers to serve static assets with automatic edge caching?
questions.explanation: Cloudflare Pages provides a static site hosting platform that integrates tightly with Workers for edge logic.
questions.source_text: Which Cloudflare product would you pair with Workers to serve static assets with automatic edge caching?

questions.title: When deploying a Worker to a specific subdomain (e.g., api.example.com), which wrangler.toml property should you set?
questions.explanation: The `routes` array defines URL patterns (including subdomains) that trigger the Worker.
questions.source_text: When deploying a Worker to a specific subdomain (e.g., api.example.com), which wrangler.toml property should you set?

questions.title: What is the purpose of the `workers_dev` flag in wrangler.toml?
options: A. Enable a custom domain for the Worker
B. Deploy the Worker to a preview subdomain on cloudflare.dev
C. Allow the Worker to run in development mode locally
D. Disable Cloudflare analytics for the Worker
questions.explanation: `workers_dev: true` tells Wrangler to publish the Worker to a workers.dev subdomain for testing.
questions.source_text: What is the purpose of the `workers_dev` flag in wrangler.toml?

questions.title: Which HTTP response header can be set in a Worker to control client‑side caching?
questions.explanation: `Cache-Control` is the standard header to dictate how browsers cache the response.
questions.source_text: Which HTTP response header can be set in a Worker to control client‑side caching?
